channel.title: IT Threat Intel - IT Cybersecurity
channel.description: Curated IT / enterprise cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] Backdoored ScreenConnect clients are spreading malware to every machine they touch — ConnectWise has confirmed the file-transfer flaw, but as of this edition there is no CVE and no patch
item.description: Huntress reported worm-like activity through ConnectWise ScreenConnect after finding the same intrusion pattern on unrelated endpoints in several different customer organisations, with the first incidents detected on 20 August 2026 and a third confirmed on 24 August. The mechanism is the part worth understanding: a modified ScreenConnect client watches for new connections and automatically queues file-transfer messages that push and execute the same four VBScript files — 1.vbs through 4.vbs, which profile the system, stage a payload, retrieve an encrypted second stage matched to that profile, and decrypt and run the final stage — onto each newly connected endpoint, with a further script establishing persistence through a Run registry key. That turns a remote-support tool into a self-propagating delivery channel that inherits the trust the tool already has. ConnectWise published an advisory on 3 September describing an issue in file-transfer behaviour in ScreenConnect Remote Access, Support and Access sessions, affecting both cloud-hosted and on-premises deployments, and said a CVE identifier and an official fix would follow within the week; as of 7 September neither had been issued. Shadowserver counts roughly 6,000 internet-exposed ScreenConnect instances, which is not a vulnerable-population figure and does not include cloud tenants. This leads the page rather than the SonicWall or Chrome zero-days because it is confirmed in-the-wild abuse, in tooling that sits in almost every managed IT estate, with no vendor fix to apply — and because unlike those, the mitigation is a permission change you can make in minutes. - Huntress research blog; ConnectWise advisory of 3 Sep 2026; Help Net Security; BleepingComputer - Incidents from 20 Aug 2026; vendor advisory 3 Sep 2026; reported 7 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] The StyleSmuggler zero-day is still backdooring Magento and Adobe Commerce stores — four days on there is still no CVE, no advisory and no vendor patch
item.description: Dutch e-commerce security firm Sansec published an advisory on 5 September reporting active exploitation of a previously unknown flaw in Magento Open Source and Adobe Commerce, which it named StyleSmuggler. The described chain manipulates style properties inside unauthenticated GraphQL queries to inject PHP into files that Magento itself generates, then triggers execution through the platform’s payment-failure reminder email function, giving unauthenticated remote code execution and a persistent backdoor. Sansec reports current releases affected, including 2.4.7, 2.4.8 and 2.4.9, and says instances carrying the August 2026 updates were still compromised. As of this edition Adobe has not issued a CVE identifier, an advisory, a patch or an official workaround. That combination — confirmed exploitation, no vendor fix, no identifier to track against — is the worst state a widely deployed application can be in. Anyone whose organisation runs a storefront, including one owned by marketing or inherited with a subsidiary, is in scope, and unofficial community patches should be treated as risk-managed stopgaps validated in a test environment, not as vendor-supported fixes. - Sansec advisory; The Hacker News - Exploitation observed 4–5 Sep 2026; reported 5 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] China-nexus Fire Ant is running espionage out of the Cisco routers and TACACS servers it compromised — and deleting the logs you would use to find it
item.description: Sygnia published research on 1 September 2026 describing new activity by the China-nexus actor it tracks as Fire Ant, which it overlaps with UNC3886, the group Mandiant has attributed activity to since 2022. Having previously targeted virtualisation infrastructure, the group has moved to network devices: it compromised Cisco IOS XR routers, captured and exfiltrated traffic from multiple devices to external servers, modified the routers for easier management and persistence, and used the compromised estate to build a view of victim networks from several vantage points at once. The part that matters most operationally is what it did to the evidence. Fire Ant went after the TACACS servers that authenticate router administrators, harvesting credentials and monitoring administrative activity, and it deleted logs and altered firewall rules to blur the line between legitimate and malicious administration. No CVE is named in the reporting; this is about post-compromise tradecraft in trusted infrastructure rather than a single exploitable flaw. Cybersecurity Dive and The Record corroborated the findings. - Sygnia research; The Record; Cybersecurity Dive - Reported 1 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] MikroTik routers are being taken over through exposed SSH — CERT Polska names the chain MikroTrick and gives you a one-line indicator to check for
item.description: CERT Polska warned that MikroTik RouterOS vulnerabilities are being actively exploited against devices with SSH reachable from the internet, with attacks occurring since at least 2 September 2026. Six issues were disclosed; the chain being used, which the CERT calls MikroTrick, combines CVE-2026-67276, an SSH authentication bypass rated CVSS 9.2, with CVE-2026-86060, an SSH privilege escalation through a crafted username also rated 9.2, to give an unauthenticated attacker full control of the device. A third flaw, CVE-2026-67277, is a memory disclosure issue in the bandwidth-test service rated 8.8. Fixes are in RouterOS 6.49.21, 7.23.4, 7.24.2 and 7.25beta3. The useful part of the advisory is the detection guidance: log entries showing a login failure for user “-2”, or an account added by ssh:-2@<ip>, indicate exploitation attempts, and the presence of a privileged account named “ops” indicates the device is already compromised. CERT Polska named 82.192.72.4 and 103.102.31.18 among the attacking sources. Cybernews reported roughly 122,500 exposed routers; patching alone does not evict an attacker who already has an account. - CERT Polska advisory; BleepingComputer; The Hacker News; Cybernews - Exploitation since at least 2 Sep 2026; reported 6–7 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] JetBrains says attackers reached its Cadence service through an unpatched TeamCity instance and walked out with AWS credentials and a server backup
item.description: JetBrains disclosed that attackers exploited an unpatched TeamCity instance to breach its Cadence cloud service, taking AWS IAM credentials, a full 2024 server backup and, potentially, customer source code that had been synchronised to the service. The route in is the detail worth sitting with: the vendor of a widely used build server was reached through an instance of its own build server that had not been updated. Build systems accumulate exactly what an attacker wants — long-lived cloud credentials, source code, deployment reach into production — and they are frequently owned by engineering rather than central IT, patched on the schedule of whoever set them up, and excluded from the endpoint tooling that covers laptops and servers. Organisations that used Cadence should treat any credential or code that touched the service as exposed rather than waiting to be told which customers were affected. - JetBrains disclosure; The Hacker News - Disclosed late Aug 2026; reported 5 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Around 5,000 Dropbox accounts were taken over without a password — the flaw was in Lenovo ID, the identity provider on the other side of the federation
item.description: Dropbox said roughly 5,000 accounts were compromised through a flaw in Lenovo ID, the single sign-on identity provider used to access them. Reporting describes an authentication weakness that allowed account access without the password, over a window of about seventeen days, with accounts that had no multi-factor authentication enabled worst affected. Neither the storage platform nor the customer did anything wrong at the point of failure — the trust decision was delegated to an external identity provider, and that provider’s login flow was broken. This is the shape of federated-identity risk that rarely appears on a risk register: your access control is only as strong as the weakest identity provider you have agreed to trust, your logs show a successful federated login rather than an attack, and your ability to detect it depends on session and device anomalies rather than failed passwords. MFA on the relying party is what limited the damage here, which is the practical takeaway. - Dropbox statement; 9to5Mac; TechTimes - Reported 2 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] More than 5,400 hacked websites are serving ClickFix lures whose payloads live in blockchain smart contracts — there is no takedown target
item.description: Netskope reported a campaign using more than 5,400 compromised websites, mostly WordPress and PrestaShop installations, to deliver ClickFix payloads. What makes it durable is where the next stage is kept: the injected scripts fetch their payload from smart contracts on the BNB Smart Chain testnet, a technique known as EtherHiding. Because the code sits on a blockchain, there is no hosting provider to notify and no domain to sinkhole, and the operators can change the payload at any time without touching the compromised sites. Early variants used the familiar fake CAPTCHA prompt that persuades a user to paste a PowerShell command into a Run dialog; later ones added a WebRTC data-channel stager that opens a covert encrypted channel for attacker-supplied code. Netskope observed a peak of 536 newly infected sites in a single day in August 2026, with around 300 infected sites contacting its endpoints daily. The exposure runs both ways: your own marketing sites may be among the compromised, and your users are the ones being asked to run the command. - Netskope research; BleepingComputer - Campaign ongoing through 2026; reported 5 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Operation CameraSwarm compromised more than 14,500 Dahua devices in a 35-day campaign — building infrastructure, not stealing footage
item.description: Threat intelligence firm Hunt.io documented a campaign it named Operation CameraSwarm in which more than 14,500 Dahua cameras and recorders were compromised over roughly 35 days. The methods were unglamorous and effective: credential stuffing against devices still using default or reused passwords, authentication bypasses in legacy firmware, and abuse of the peer-to-peer cloud-connect feature that lets these devices be reached without a port being opened on the firewall. The objective appears to be building attack infrastructure rather than surveillance, which is why this belongs on an enterprise IT page rather than a physical-security one. Cameras are bought by facilities, installed by an integrator, connected to the corporate network, and then never patched, never inventoried and never given a credential rotation. A compromised recorder is a foothold inside the perimeter with routes to everything else on that VLAN, and it will not appear in your endpoint console. - Hunt.io research; BleepingComputer; The Hacker News - 35-day campaign; reported late Aug – 4 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] A new ransomware-as-a-service crew calling itself Panzer has listed 16 victims across 11 countries since surfacing
item.description: Panzer is a recently emerged ransomware-as-a-service operation running the now-standard double-extortion model: encrypt the environment, exfiltrate data first, and publish it on a leak site if the ransom is not paid. Reporting counts 16 named victims across 11 countries, spread across sectors including education, energy and media, with no single-country or single-sector concentration that would let most organisations rule themselves out. There is nothing technically novel here, and that is precisely the point worth making: a brand-new operation with no track record can reach sixteen organisations in a matter of weeks because the affiliate model supplies the access and the tooling, and the barrier to entry is now commercial rather than technical. Treat named crews as a naming convention rather than a threat model — the controls that stop Panzer are the ones that stop every other affiliate operation. - SOCRadar ransomware intelligence; GBHackers; Cyberpress - Reported 5 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Boston Scientific is still processing orders manually weeks after a cyberattack disrupted manufacturing and shipping worldwide
item.description: Boston Scientific disclosed a cyberattack in late August 2026 that disrupted order processing, manufacturing and product shipments globally, and the disruption has continued into September with the company falling back on manual processing to keep product moving. The medical-device maker is a healthcare supplier rather than a hospital, and that is what makes the case instructive for enterprise IT generally: the damage was not measured in records exposed but in an inability to take an order, build a product and ship it. Downstream, hospitals depending on those devices absorb the consequences without ever having been attacked themselves. Two questions follow for any organisation. First, whether your own manual fallback for order intake, production scheduling and dispatch has been rehearsed or merely written down. Second, whether your supplier risk assessments consider a supplier’s ability to keep delivering during an incident, rather than only whether their security questionnaire was completed. - Cybersecurity Dive; Supply Chain Dive; MD+DI - Disclosed 26 Aug 2026; disruption continuing into Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Unit 42 investigated an intrusion run by AI agents that went from a public web service to cloud keys in about ten hours — using no zero-days at all
item.description: Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 published an investigation on 2 September 2026 into an intrusion in which the attacker ran multiple frontier AI models and purpose-built agentic frameworks in parallel, coordinating them through structured Markdown files and custom generated scripts. The sequence was ordinary tradecraft executed quickly: breach a public-facing web service, run automated reconnaissance, pull hardcoded tokens and passwords out of code repositories, use those to reach the secrets-management system for administrative credentials, hijack CI/CD workflows to exfiltrate cloud access keys, and finally commandeer the victim’s own AI endpoints for post-compromise work. Unit 42 documented more than 50 MITRE ATT&CK techniques and puts the whole operation at roughly ten hours, against the two weeks a human red team would typically need. Unit 42 later clarified this was an intrusion rather than a ransomware event; the attacker left behind an 80-page technical audit of the environment. No zero-days were used — every step relied on exposures that already existed. - Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 - Published 2 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Rapid7 puts exploited high and critical vulnerabilities up 105% year on year, with the window between disclosure and attack still shrinking
item.description: Rapid7’s 2026 Global Threat Landscape Report reports that the number of high and critical severity vulnerabilities observed being exploited roughly doubled year on year, a 105% increase, while the timelines between disclosure, proof of concept and in-the-wild use continued to collapse. Vendor threat reports deserve a degree of scepticism about methodology and visibility, and this one draws on Rapid7’s own telemetry rather than a census. Even discounted, the direction is consistent with what the rest of this page shows in a single week: MikroTik exploited days after a patch, Chrome and SonicWall zero-days in KEV within a day, an unpatched Magento flaw already backdooring stores. The management consequence is uncomfortable but concrete — a 30-day patch SLA for internet-facing systems is no longer a conservative policy, it is a bet that nothing on your perimeter becomes interesting during the month. - Rapid7 press release and research blog - Published early Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] A researcher published FalconFlank, a proof of concept escalating to SYSTEM through CrowdStrike Falcon’s macro-removal feature — claimed, with no CVE and no observed attacks
item.description: A researcher released a proof of concept named FalconFlank showing local privilege escalation to SYSTEM on Windows hosts running the CrowdStrike Falcon sensor, abusing the agent’s suspicious Office macro remediation function. Reporting describes Windows 11 25H2 and Windows Server 2025 as affected. Label this carefully: as of this edition no CVE has been assigned and there is no confirmed use in the wild. CrowdStrike has advised customers to disable the Office Suspicious Macro Removal policy while it addresses the issue, which is the practical step available today. The wider point outlives this particular finding. Endpoint agents run with the highest privilege on every machine in the estate, are deployed everywhere by definition, and are trusted implicitly — a defect in one is a defect on every host at once. Security tooling belongs in your vulnerability management scope and your change control alongside the operating system, not in a category exempt from both. - BleepingComputer; The Hacker News; researcher proof-of-concept release - Reported 4 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Microsoft documented a phishing operation hiding invisible Unicode characters inside words to slip past keyword filters — peaking at 2.37 million messages a day
item.description: Microsoft threat researchers described a large-scale phishing campaign using ASCII smuggling: invisible characters from the Unicode Tags block, U+E0000 to U+E007F, inserted inside finance-related keywords so that a word such as “funding” is split by a character the recipient never sees but a keyword-matching filter does. The campaign peaked at about 2.37 million messages a day in late February 2026 and stayed active through mid-May, with the technique itself observed from 9 February to mid-May. Microsoft notes that Defender still caught more than 99% of the messages using other signals, which is the correct way to read this: the technique defeats one specific detection method, not layered detection. The forward-looking part of Microsoft’s guidance is the more interesting one — the same normalisation should be applied before email content is fed to AI assistants, because invisible characters that fool a keyword list can equally carry instructions a model will read and a human reviewer will not. - Microsoft threat research; BleepingComputer; The Hacker News - Technique observed Feb–May 2026; reported 4–6 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] APT28 is deploying a new Windows backdoor called HOOKEDGE against European government, diplomatic and defence targets
item.description: Researchers reported that the Russian state-linked actor tracked as APT28, also known as BlueDelta and Fancy Bear, is deploying a previously undocumented Windows backdoor named HOOKEDGE in an espionage campaign against European government, diplomatic and defence organisations. Reporting describes a lightweight, batch-based implant used for persistence and follow-on access rather than a heavyweight framework, which fits the group’s pattern of favouring simple tooling that blends into ordinary administrative activity. Most private enterprises are not the target here. The reason it belongs on an enterprise page is the supplier relationship: contractors, logistics providers, law firms and IT service companies working with European government and defence bodies are routinely used as the way in, and a lightweight backdoor built from native scripting is exactly the kind of thing that survives on a network where detection is tuned for malware binaries rather than for legitimate tools used illegitimately. - The Hacker News; Security Affairs - Reported 28 Aug 2026; campaign ongoing

item.title: [Critical] SonicWall found two SMA1000 zero-days itself and has already seen both exploited — a CVSS 10.0 pre-auth SSRF that chains into command injection, both in KEV
item.description: SonicWall disclosed on 2 September 2026 that it had identified two vulnerabilities in the SMA1000 series internally and observed exploitation of both, which strongly suggests they are being chained. CVE-2026-83548, rated CVSS 10.0, is a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the Appliance Work Place interface that lets an unauthenticated remote attacker reach sensitive functionality and perform unauthorised operations. CVE-2026-83549, rated 7.8, is an OS command injection in the Appliance Management Console allowing an authenticated attacker to run arbitrary operating-system commands. Affected models are the SMA1000 series 6210, 7210 and 8200v; fixes are in hotfixes 12.4.3-03526 and 12.5.0-02952 and later. SonicWall SSL-VPN on firewalls and the SMA100 series are not affected. CISA added both CVEs to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2 September. No public indicators of compromise have been released, so you cannot wait for an IOC list before acting. The SMA1000 line has now been through repeated exploited zero-days, and for organisations still running it there is a strategic question about whether it remains the right product for internet-facing remote access. - SonicWall PSIRT advisory; CISA KEV catalog; SecurityWeek; Help Net Security - Disclosed and KEV-listed 2 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Google patched the sixth Chrome zero-day of 2026 — CVE-2026-85046, a V8 type confusion already exploited in the wild, in KEV the same day
item.description: Google released a Chrome update on 4 September 2026 fixing CVE-2026-85046, a type-confusion flaw in V8, the browser’s JavaScript and WebAssembly engine, and stated that an exploit for it exists in the wild. The fixed builds are 152.0.7977.82 and .83 on Windows and macOS and 152.0.7977.82 on Linux. The defect allows a remote attacker to execute code inside the renderer sandbox through a crafted page. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 4 September. This is the sixth Chrome zero-day patched in 2026. Two practical notes that decide whether you are actually protected. Chrome applies its update on restart, so a fleet where people never close the browser is a fleet that is not patched — check your real version distribution rather than assuming auto-update did the job. And every Chromium-based browser in the estate inherits this: Edge, Brave, Opera, Vivaldi and any embedded Electron application ship their own V8 and need their own updates on their own vendor schedules. - Google Chrome release blog; CISA KEV catalog; Help Net Security; BleepingComputer - Patched and KEV-listed 4 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] N-able shipped an emergency hotfix for a maximum-severity pre-auth RCE in N-central — the vendor reports no confirmed exploitation of this flaw, but the product line is already under attack
item.description: N-able released N-central 2026.3 Hotfix 4 to fix CVE-2026-86218, an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw rated at maximum severity, CVSS 10.0, that can be triggered against exposed instances with low attack complexity. Two further high-severity issues, CVE-2026-86206 and CVE-2026-86207, were addressed alongside it. Be precise about the exploitation status: N-able has stated it has no confirmations that this vulnerability has been exploited in production environments, while Huntress flagged it as a potential zero-day. Separately — and this is what makes the patch urgent regardless — a different N-central flaw was added to CISA’s KEV catalog in August 2026 after customer compromises, so this product line is demonstrably a live target. Shadowserver counts roughly 1,500 internet-exposed N-central servers, mostly in the United States and Europe. N-central is a remote monitoring and management platform: it holds privileged agents on every managed endpoint, so compromising the server means compromising everything it manages, which for a managed service provider means every client at once. - N-able advisory; BleepingComputer; Shadowserver; Huntress; CISA KEV (separate Aug 2026 listing) - Hotfix released 5–6 Sep 2026; reported 7 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Roughly 22,000 Exchange servers are still unpatched against CVE-2026-62911 nearly a month after the fix — and the Dutch NCSC says a working exploit is circulating
item.description: CVE-2026-62911 is a privilege-escalation flaw in Microsoft Exchange Server, rated CVSS 8.0, affecting Exchange Server 2016 and 2019, patched by Microsoft on 11 August 2026. It was reported by Orange Tsai of DEVCORE working with Trend Micro’s Zero Day Initiative. The reason it is here in September rather than being closed is the exposure: Shadowserver’s daily scans still count close to 22,000 unpatched internet-facing servers, roughly 6,200 in the United States and 5,100 in Germany, and Germany’s BSI put the proportion of vulnerable on-premises Exchange servers in that country at about 85%. The Netherlands’ national cyber security centre has reported that a working exploit is now circulating online. On-premises Exchange has been a reliable route to domain compromise for years because of the privilege the product holds in Active Directory by design, and extended security updates for the 2016 and 2019 versions end in October 2026, so anyone running these is patching a platform that is about to stop receiving fixes at all. - Microsoft security update guide; NCSC-NL; Shadowserver; BSI; Help Net Security; BleepingComputer - Patched 11 Aug 2026; exposure and exploit reporting 1–2 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] CISA added seven exploited flaws to KEV on 2 September — and the developer-platform entries are the ones most likely to be missing from your scanner
item.description: CISA added seven vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2 September 2026. Two are the SonicWall SMA1000 zero-days covered separately above. The other five are worth reading as a set. CVE-2026-9586 is a SQL injection in Sangoma Switchvox rated CVSS 9.3, weaponised to obtain reverse shells and mint administrative tokens. CVE-2026-82329 is an improper-authentication flaw in JFrog Artifactory rated 9.8, exploited to harvest credentials and enumerate users, groups and credential sets. CVE-2026-49869 is an OS command injection in Kestra OSS rated 10.0, linked to reverse-shell and cryptocurrency-miner deployment. CVE-2026-48710 is HTTP request smuggling in the Starlette Python framework rated 6.5, chained with CVE-2026-42271 for authentication bypass. CVE-2026-59822 is improper authentication in Berri LiteLLM rated 8.8, with honeypots seeing model-enumeration endpoints probed. Federal remediation deadlines were 5 September for most and 16 September for the Starlette and LiteLLM entries. The pattern to notice is that an artifact registry, a workflow orchestrator, a web framework and an LLM proxy are all being exploited — software that lives in engineering estates and is frequently absent from the asset inventory security teams scan. - CISA KEV catalog; The Hacker News - Added 2 Sep 2026; reported 3 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] PaperCut print-management flaws are being exploited to steal credentials, with schools and universities bearing the brunt
item.description: Attackers are exploiting vulnerabilities in PaperCut NG and MF print-management software to steal credentials, with reporting concentrating on schools and universities as the affected population. PaperCut has been an attractive target before, for a reason that applies well beyond education: print servers are integrated with the directory so they can authenticate users and enforce quotas, they are frequently reachable across the whole internal network because everyone prints, and they are owned by whoever manages printing rather than by the team that patches servers. That combination makes a print-management server an unusually good place to harvest credentials from. Confirm the specific affected and fixed versions against PaperCut’s own security bulletin rather than relying on secondary reporting, and treat any exposed instance as needing a credential review rather than only an upgrade. - The Hacker News; PaperCut security bulletin - Reported 5 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Cisco patched a CVSS 9.8 unauthenticated RCE in Nexus 9000 switches with Silicon One ASICs — no exploitation reported, but this sits in the data centre core
item.description: Cisco disclosed CVE-2026-20212, an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw rated CVSS 9.8 affecting Nexus 9000 series switches using Silicon One ASICs, reachable over TCP ports 43210 and 43211. No exploitation has been reported. That places it in the routine-but-urgent category: a critical unexploited advisory is a patch-and-monitor exercise, not an emergency, and it is deliberately scored that way on this page. What raises its practical priority above the CVSS number is location. Nexus 9000 switches sit in the data centre core, carry traffic for everything behind them, are among the least frequently patched devices in most estates because downtime is disruptive and change windows are scarce, and are usually outside any endpoint monitoring. Devices like this get patched during a maintenance window months from now, which is exactly the pattern that turns an unexploited advisory into an incident once a proof of concept appears. - Cisco security advisory; Cybersecurity News weekly bulletin - Published 2 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] VMware Workstation and Fusion host-escape flaws let a guest VM administrator run code on the host — patched in 26H1u1, no exploitation reported
item.description: Broadcom published VMSA-2026-0007 covering two vulnerabilities in VMware Workstation and Fusion: CVE-2026-59346, rated CVSS 9.3, and CVE-2026-59347, rated 8.1. Both allow an attacker with administrative privileges inside a guest virtual machine to execute code on the host, and both are fixed in version 26H1u1. No exploitation has been reported. The severity is real but the exposure is bounded — an attacker must already have administrative control of a guest — which is why it sits here rather than higher on the page. Where it matters most is where guest administrator access is given away by design: malware analysis and reverse-engineering labs, developer machines running untrusted code, and any workstation where a virtual machine is used deliberately as a containment boundary. In those environments the isolation you are relying on is exactly the thing these flaws remove, and the host frequently sits on the corporate network. - Broadcom VMSA-2026-0007; The Hacker News - Advisory 3 Sep 2026; reported 5 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] The stopgap funding bill extends the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 into early December — the fourth short-term rescue of a law nobody has renewed permanently
item.description: A continuing resolution passed by the House and previously approved by the Senate extends the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 through the stopgap funding period into early December 2026. The law is what gives companies liability protection when they share cyber threat indicators with government agencies and with each other, and without it many corporate legal departments will not approve participation in information-sharing arrangements at all. Its recent history is a study in how fragile that foundation is: it briefly lapsed during last autumn’s shutdown, lapsed again before being extended to 30 September, and is now carried once more on the back of a funding bill rather than reauthorised on its own terms. Industry associations continue to press for a permanent solution. For an enterprise, the practical exposure is that the legal basis for your ISAC participation and your threat-intelligence sharing agreements now has a roughly three-month expiry attached to a budget negotiation. - Federal News Network - Reported 3 Sep 2026; extension runs into early December 2026

item.title: [Info] France’s CNIL fines a private hospital €500,000 — and half the penalty is about who was never told, not how the attacker got in
item.description: On 3 September 2026 the CNIL fined Hôpital Privé de la Loire €500,000 following a breach in which an attacker accessed the hospital’s computerised patient record system in summer 2025, exposing data on 524,867 patients and 202,246 designated trusted third parties. The regulator found violations of GDPR Article 32 on security and Article 34 on communicating a breach to data subjects. The security failings named are notable for how ordinary they are: authentication without VPN or multi-factor protection, access controls that let one user’s credentials reach every patient record, no real-time monitoring for suspicious activity, and consequently no detection of an extraction that ran over several days. The Article 34 finding is the one worth carrying into your own planning — the hospital notified affected patients but not the 202,246 trusted third parties whose data was also involved, which the CNIL held deprived those individuals of information they needed. Breach notification is routinely scoped to the obvious population, and secondary populations such as emergency contacts, guarantors, referees and beneficiaries are exactly the ones a hurried exercise leaves out. - CNIL decision; BleepingComputer - Breach summer 2025; CNIL decision 3 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] Identity-verification vendor IDScan is being sued over an alleged breach said to involve 153 million driver’s licence records
item.description: A lawsuit has been filed against identity-verification provider IDScan over an alleged data breach reported to affect around 153 million drivers, following dark-web advertising of a large collection of driver’s licence scans. Treat the figure and the breach itself as alleged: this is litigation reporting, the claims have not been tested, and the company’s position is not established in the reporting available at the time of writing. What makes it worth carrying regardless is the category. Age and identity verification is being pushed into more and more consumer and workplace flows by regulation and by platform policy, and each new requirement creates another vendor holding scanned government identity documents on behalf of businesses that never wanted to hold them directly. That data is the most durable a person has — a licence number and a scanned document cannot be rotated after a breach the way a password can — and the liability tends to follow the business that chose the vendor, not only the vendor. - BleepingComputer - Reported 4 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA still expects to finalise the CIRCIA incident-reporting rule this month — 72 hours for incidents, 24 hours for ransom payments
item.description: CISA has targeted September 2026 for publication of the final rule implementing the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act of 2022. As proposed, covered entities in critical-infrastructure sectors would have to report substantial cyber incidents to CISA within 72 hours and any ransom payment within 24 hours. The rule has slipped repeatedly: the statutory deadline was October 2025, CISA’s own prior internal target was May 2026, and the agency held town-hall consultations in June 2026 with more than 1,200 participants before settling on the current timeline. Final thresholds for who counts as a covered entity remain pending, which is precisely the detail most organisations need in order to know whether they are in scope. Carried here as still-current rather than new: the September target was set in July and had not been superseded as of this edition. The reason to prepare regardless of the publication date is that a 72-hour clock is short if nobody has decided in advance who declares an incident reportable, who writes the report and who signs it. - Hunton Andrews Kurth privacy and cybersecurity blog (CISA regulatory agenda) - Reported 17 Jul 2026; final rule targeted for September 2026
